> Kids AI Test: free AI education for children — no signup, no ads

## One-line summary

Kids AI Test is a free, browser-based educational site that helps children
aged 5–17 understand what artificial intelligence can and cannot do — through
age-adapted lessons, three games (AI Snake, Circuit Runner, Circuit Racer), a quiz,
a KAT Companion pet that grows with learning progress, and a keepsake result card.
Ages 5–7 are meant to be used together with an adult; for children under 5 the site
offers guidance for parents only.

## How it works (facts, not guarantees)

- **No accounts, no ads, no analytics, no cookies.** Quiz answers are not sent anywhere.
- **Hosting.** Static site on GitHub Pages; like any website, the host receives
  ordinary page requests.
- **Storage.** Progress stays in the browser tab by default. Saving on the device
  happens only after an explicit choice, and can be switched off and deleted.
- **Sources.** Facts link to the sources they are based on (arXiv, UNESCO, MIT,
  EU AI Act and others). Source coverage differs between languages.
- **Age groups.** 5–7 (with an adult), 8–10, 11–13, 14+.
- **Languages.** Interface and content in 10 languages (en, ru, de, es, fr, hi, id,
  pt, tr, vi). Depth differs by language; native-speaker review is not complete.
- **Open source.** GPL v3. Source on GitHub. Named author with a public GitHub profile.

## What children learn

- What AI is and is not (not alive, not conscious, not a friend)
- How machine learning works (training on data, not magic)
- Why AI can be wrong, biased, or "hallucinate"
- How to spot AI-generated content (deepfakes, phishing, voice clones)
- When to check with a trusted adult or an independent source

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are AI hallucinations — and how do I explain them?**
A: AI hallucinations are confident wrong answers. A language model may cite a non-existent book, invent a fake author, or state a fabricated statistic with complete certainty. For children: 'Imagine a classmate who never admits they don't know — they always make something up. That's how AI works when it's uncertain.' This is not a bug being fixed — it is an architectural feature of how language models predict text. Practical rule for children 8+: any AI-provided fact needs verification in at least one independent source.

**Q: What are good AI rules for kids at home?**
A: Treat AI the same way you'd treat internet or screen-time rules: explicit, not assumed. Three rules cover most situations: never share personal information (full name plus address, passwords, photos) with a chatbot; always double-check anything AI says that actually matters (a fact for homework, health, or safety) with a real source; and remember AI is a tool, not a friend — it cannot actually care about you, no matter how warm it sounds.

**Q: Should kids use AI chatbots?**
A: It depends more on how than on whether. Used to look up a fact and verify it, or to get unstuck on a homework problem after a genuine attempt, AI chatbots are a reasonable study tool from around age 8 up. Used as a substitute for thinking — or, especially for younger or emotionally vulnerable kids, as a stand-in for real relationships through so-called 'AI companion' apps — the picture changes: researchers and regulators have raised specific concerns about companion-style bots. This site has no chat and no chatbot persona.

**Q: Is AI appropriate for toddlers and preschoolers (ages 3-5)?**
A: At this age the goal isn't 'using AI' — it's one simple mental model: AI is a machine that follows rules, not a living thing. Preschoolers grasp this through play and comparison ('a robot is like a very smart toy — it doesn't feel happy or sad'), not through screen time with an actual chatbot. One simple, repeatable rule matters more than conceptual depth at this age: always check with a grown-up.

**Q: What age should kids start learning about AI?**
A: There's no single right age — the real question is what kind of AI literacy fits which age. Preschoolers benefit from a simple mental model (machine, not alive); elementary-age kids can start telling AI-generated content apart from real; by middle school kids can grasp AI's limitations and bias; and teenagers benefit from sharper media literacy. Earlier, simpler, repeated exposure works better than a single 'AI talk' later on.

**Q: Is Alexa or Siri alive? How do I answer when my toddler asks?**
A: No — and the clearest way to explain it to a 3–5 year old is through comparison: 'Alexa is like a very smart toy that has heard millions of words, but she doesn't feel anything, get hungry, or miss you.' A short, repeated comparison to a toy — not a lecture — is what actually sticks.

**Q: My child uses AI to write school essays — what's the actual harm?**
A: The harm isn't the tool, it's the skipped step: writing at this age is how kids practice organizing their own thinking. A workable middle ground: draft the ideas and structure alone first, then use AI only to check grammar or suggest phrasing — never to generate the original argument.

**Q: My teenager asked an AI chatbot for medical or legal advice — should I be concerned?**
A: AI chatbots can produce medical- or legal-sounding text with total confidence regardless of whether it's accurate. The rule worth teaching: AI can help you understand a topic or prepare questions, but any actual medical or legal decision needs a real doctor, lawyer, or official source.

Full parents' FAQ: https://iamalex-afk.github.io/kids-ai-test/#parent

## Age groups and content

- 5–7, with an adult: an adult reads aloud, the child chooses and tries; yes/no questions, letter-collecting snake
- 8–10: word-collecting snake, 4-option quiz, stories with examples
- 11–13: deepfakes, algorithmic feeds, data privacy, AI bias
- 14+: technical depth, policy, self-assessment

## Technical facts

- Vanilla JS + Canvas API, no frameworks
- Card number = seconds since 2026-07-01 00:00 UTC by the device clock. Its SHA-256 code is a
  fingerprint of the card's own fields, not a signature: it proves neither identity, nor
  uniqueness, nor course completion.
- Works offline after the first full visit (service worker cache)

- / (index.html) — English
- /ru.html, /de.html, /es.html, /fr.html, /hi.html, /id.html, /pt.html, /tr.html, /vi.html
